passage:
Aditi had stopped choosing her own lunch. She texted Vishal before she picked a shirt, before she replied to a group message, and when he was in a lab she felt like a room with the light off. Her old friend Mehak had invited her to a pottery class twice, and Aditi had said "maybe" both times. She could not remember when she last did anything without asking him first.

Vishal loved her, and he felt the weight of it. His phone buzzed through lectures, and if he did not answer for an hour, the next message said "Are you upset with me?" He found himself dreading the buzz and feeling guilty for dreading it. One evening he said, gently, "I care about you a lot. I can't be your only person, and I don't think you'd want that either. What about the pottery class Mehak keeps mentioning?"

Aditi went quiet, stung and a little frightened. Then she realised that he had not pushed her away. He had opened a door. On Saturday she went to the class with Mehak, got clay on her sleeve and laughed. When she came home and told him about it, he listened without checking the time.

qa.q: Who kept inviting Aditi to a pottery class?
qa.a: Mehak kept inviting her to the pottery class.

qa.q: How did Aditi's leaning and Vishal's reaction fit together, and what changed after he spoke?
qa.a: Aditi texted Vishal about everything and felt like a dark room without him, while he felt the weight and dreaded the buzz. When Vishal kindly named his limit and mentioned Mehak's pottery class, Aditi tried it and built something of her own.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when his phone kept buzzing during lectures?
qa.a: He felt weighed down, dreading the buzz and guilty for dreading it.

qa.q: What could Aditi do to keep love a choice rather than a need?
qa.a: She can keep her own friends like Mehak, and her own interests and goals, and not ask Vishal about every decision.

grounding: A partner's heavy dependence is seen from the one who leans and feels lost alone and the one who feels the weight and names a limit kindly.

passage:
When Rajni announced Pradeep's promotion to team lead, the office clapped. Tanvir clapped too, and a sour twist went through his stomach. He had joined the company the same month. That evening he said, "Congratulations, honestly. You earned it." Then he went home and spent an hour looking at what Pradeep had done differently: the client presentations, the weekend reports no one asked for. He wrote his own goals on a sheet, and put a date next to each. He did not say anything about Pradeep to anyone else.

Pradeep had felt a chill in the corridor. Tanvir had stopped sitting next to him at lunch. He did not apologise for the promotion, and he did not talk about it. He asked, "Would you look at my dashboard? You always see things I miss," and he told Rajni in front of the team that Tanvir had helped him set up the reporting system last year. Tanvir looked down at his plate.

Nothing changed that week. Pradeep kept sending him the occasional link to an article he'd like, without expecting an answer, and told himself that distance might be grief. A month later, Tanvir slid into the seat opposite him with his tray and said, "I've picked a course to sign up for. Want to hear what it is?"

qa.q: What did Rajni announce at the office?
qa.a: Rajni announced Pradeep's promotion to team lead.

qa.q: How did Tanvir's envy and Pradeep's response fit together?
qa.a: Tanvir felt a sour twist but congratulated Pradeep and turned to his own goals. Pradeep sensed the chill, did not apologise or flaunt, credited Tanvir's help, and gave the friendship time.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling as he clapped for Pradeep?
qa.a: He felt envious and sour in the stomach, since they had joined the company the same month.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do if Tanvir stays distant for longer than a month?
qa.a: He can stay warm without flaunting his promotion, keep small gestures, and understand the distance may be grief, not hatred.

grounding: A colleague's promotion is seen from the peer who feels envy and the promoted friend who senses a chill and stays warm.

passage:
Jasleen had forgotten to pick up Leela's mother at the station, and she had waited in the rain for forty minutes. Leela's heart pounded when she got home. The cruelest true thing was ready on her tongue, about how Jasleen always got distracted, how he was just like his father. She saw his face, and she stopped. "I'm too angry to talk right now. I'm going out for a walk, and I'll come back in twenty minutes." On the stairs she met Tushar, the neighbour, who looked at her flushed face and said nothing, just held the door.

Jasleen stood in the hallway and felt the fear that she might be about to lose her. His first thoughts were the excuses: I thought she said seven, the phone was dead. He noticed them and let them go. When Leela came back, cooler, he said, "I'm ready to listen. Tell me what hurt."

She told him. "I was frightened Amma would be standing there alone. And I felt like I couldn't count on you. Next time, please text me if you can't make it." Jasleen nodded. "I should have set an alarm and I didn't. I'm sorry." She put a hand on his arm, and they went to make tea for her mother.

qa.q: How long did Leela's mother wait at the station?
qa.a: She waited for forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Leela's pause and Jasleen's listening fit together?
qa.a: Leela was flooded with anger but stepped out for a walk instead of saying the cruelest true thing. Jasleen felt afraid of losing her, let his excuses go and asked what hurt, then owned his part.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling in the hallway while Leela was out?
qa.a: He felt afraid that he might lose her, and noticed the urge to make excuses.

qa.q: What could Leela do if she is angry again and cannot find calm words?
qa.a: She can pause and cool off, then speak about her feeling and make a clear request instead of hurting words.

grounding: A marital argument is seen from the partner flooded with anger who pauses and the partner who listens without rushing to justify.

passage:
When Nikita got married, Indu sent a warm message and then went quiet. Nikita's wedding photos, her new flat, the housewarming: each one landed like a small stone in Indu's chest. She started declining invitations with "so busy at work". She noticed the avoiding and asked herself what the envy was telling her. It was not really about Nikita. It was that she wanted a home of her own, and a future she had not yet started to build. She wrote Nikita a proper message. "Sorry I've been distant. I'm truly happy for you, and I was jealous too. Coffee on Saturday?"

Nikita had felt the change already. Her messages went unanswered and her invitations came back with vague excuses. She felt awkward and lonely, half-guilty for being happy. She did not push, and she did not give up. She sent a small photo of the burnt cake from the housewarming with the caption "Vijay tried". She did not go on about the wedding. On Saturday, over coffee, she asked, "What about you, how's the job? The pottery?" and she listened to the answer for a long time.

Indu laughed at the burnt cake. She said, "I miss this. I'll come round next week and I'll bring something that isn't burnt."

qa.q: What was the caption Nikita put under the photo of the burnt cake?
qa.a: The caption was Vijay tried.

qa.q: How did Indu's distance and Nikita's response fit together?
qa.a: Indu avoided Nikita and then realised her envy showed what she wanted, so she sent an honest message. Nikita felt lonely but did not brag, sent a light photo and asked about Indu's life.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when the wedding photos landed like small stones?
qa.a: She felt jealous and sad, and that feeling was pointing to what she wanted for herself.

qa.q: What could Nikita do if Indu still cancels sometimes after this coffee?
qa.a: She can keep sharing her life without bragging, ask about Indu's, and keep it safe for Indu to be her friend.

grounding: A friend's marriage is seen from the old friend who feels envy and avoids her and the friend who senses the chill and keeps the door open.

passage:
After a brutal deadline week at work, Shankar came home and sat in front of the television without watching it. He answered Vandana's questions in single words. He did not know how to say what was wrong, because nothing about her was wrong. On Sunday morning, seeing her face, he took a breath. "I'm not upset with you. I'm just overwhelmed with work and I'm running on empty. Can we take a walk this evening, just the two of us? I'd like to be around you properly."

Vandana had felt the distance for days. She had lain awake wondering whether she'd done something, and felt lonely and rejected in her own flat. She had told her friend Lavanya over the phone, "He's somewhere else." She had not pushed for reassurance every hour. Instead, on Saturday, she said, "I miss you. I'm not trying to blame you. Is something going on for you?" Then she added, "Maybe we could just have tea together each night for ten minutes, phones away?"

Shankar looked at her. "Yes. I'd like that." On Sunday they walked around the block, not saying much, and at the end he took her hand. That night they had tea on the balcony, phones on the shelf inside.

qa.q: Who did Vandana tell over the phone that he was somewhere else?
qa.a: She told her friend Lavanya.

qa.q: How did Shankar's silence and Vandana's loneliness fit together?
qa.a: Shankar withdrew after work stress and could not say why, and Vandana felt lonely and rejected and wondered what she'd done. When she said what she missed without blame, and he named that he was overwhelmed, they made small rituals like a walk and tea.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling as she lay awake for days?
qa.a: She felt lonely and rejected, wondering whether she had done something wrong.

qa.q: What could Shankar do the next time work leaves him drained?
qa.a: He can say he is overwhelmed rather than saying nothing, and offer a small time to reconnect, like a walk.

grounding: Emotional distance after work stress is seen from the partner who withdraws and the partner who feels lonely and invites small rituals.

passage:
Kunal had been logging on at seven each morning and closing her laptop at eleven each night for two months. Gautam kept the dinner warm until it went cold. Hrithik, a colleague, noticed the shadows under her eyes and said, "Go home, it's nine." She laughed it off, then thought about the empty chair she saw every night in her mind, and did not laugh. She set an alarm for seven each evening, planned a whole Sunday with Gautam, and put her phone on the shelf when she got home.

Gautam had been feeling lonely and quietly irritated at himself for it. Kunal had become withdrawn and snappy over small things, and he did not take it as her not loving him. He said, gently, "I miss you. I know work is heavy. Could we have breakfast together on weekdays, even for fifteen minutes? And I think you need a proper rest." He did not cook every night in resentment, and he did not pretend everything was fine.

On Sunday, Kunal shut her laptop at noon and they went to the lake. She sat quietly for most of the walk. Then she said, "I've been so tired and I stopped seeing you. I'm sorry." Gautam took her hand. "I'm right here."

qa.q: At what time did Kunal set her alarm to stop work each evening?
qa.a: She set an alarm for seven each evening.

qa.q: How did Kunal's long hours and Gautam's loneliness fit together?
qa.a: Kunal's work swallowed her evenings and she became withdrawn and snappy, while Gautam felt lonely but did not take it as rejection. He said he missed her, proposed breakfast together and encouraged rest, and she set a shut-off time and planned a shared day.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling as he kept the dinner warm until it went cold?
qa.a: He felt lonely and a bit resentful, though he was careful not to blame her.

qa.q: What could Kunal do if work starts to take over her evenings again?
qa.a: She can keep the shut-off alarm and the shared Sunday, and be present when she is home instead of letting ambition crowd out connection.

grounding: Overwork in a marriage is seen from the partner who lets work swallow the evenings and the partner who feels lonely and invites small rituals.
